result.killer: The claim mixes up MUIS's own categories. According to MUIS's 2022 EE launch FAQ (Annex A) and its Category 1/2 infographic, Category 1 covers hawker stalls, snack bars, bakeries, school canteens and short-term stalls. MUIS says these 'are no longer required to establish a Halal Team and HalMQ plan', have less documentation, and hawker and school canteen stalls may buy from supermarkets. The HalMQ plan, halal team and internal audits apply to Category 2: restaurants, kiosks, halal sections, and chain, franchise and central-kitchen outlets. Chains usually run their own QA. The smallest buyers therefore have light duties. MUIS certification is also voluntary under AMLA, and MUIS's free e-service portal handles menu and ingredient submissions and renewals.
result.reason: As framed, the candidate fails. MUIS says Category 1 outlets (hawkers, bakeries, canteen and short-term stalls) are exempt from the HalMQ plan and halal team and have reduced paperwork. The heavier record-keeping falls on Category 2 restaurants and chains, and chains often have in-house QA. Certification is voluntary. The free MUIS e-service covers submissions. Generic halal-assurance software also exists: Malaysia's Dagangasia HIAS is listed on the Microsoft marketplace for SMEs. A pivot to small independent Category 2 restaurants could still be worth checking, but that market is small: MUIS said it certified more than 4,000 premises in 2016 (I found no newer figure), and that count includes manufacturers and chains. I couldn't parse the v4.1 PDFs, so whether the 2026 text kept the Category 1 exemption is unverified.

result.competitor: MOM's WSH eServices (launched 11 Aug 2023) is used by AEs to register vessels and submit examination reports, and by owners to view vessel details and reports through Corppass. It sends no reminders. AE and inspection firms such as LRQA, TUV and Munich Re HSB do the examinations and probably remind their own clients; this is unverified. Generic inspection schedulers exist (for example a Kissflow app), but I found no Singapore-specific pressure-vessel or statutory-equipment tracker. Search coverage was limited, so this is not conclusive.
result.duty: WSH (General Provisions) Regulations: owners must register pressure vessels through an AE and must engage an AE before each due date. Steam boilers are due every year; air and steam receivers and autoclaves every 2 years; autoclaves also need a 6-year external shell examination; steam receivers and packaged fire-tube boilers need a 10-year shell examination; all types need a 10-year hydrostatic test and thickness gauging. An AE can extend a due date by up to 3 months. MOM stopped sending reminder notifications from 5 Aug 2023. I could not confirm the owner's penalty for missing an examination. A 2013 circular gives fines of up to S$20k or 2 years' jail for AE misconduct, and the 2024 review raised maximum WSH fines to S$50k for serious-harm offences. The registration guidelines PDF could not be parsed.
result.market: Not found. MOM publishes no count of registered pressure vessels or owners that I could find; stats.mom.gov.sg was not checked. Air receivers, which sit with compressors in workshops, factories and F&B, are likely the largest group, probably several thousand owners. That figure is an estimate, not a sourced number. The AE register is small: AEs must be PEs in Pressure Vessel Engineering, with a list on MOM's site, which I did not count.
result.reason: The duty is real and in force. MOM requires pressure vessels to be registered through an Authorised Examiner (AE). Steam boilers must be examined every year, air and steam receivers and autoclaves every 2 years, autoclaves also get a 6-year shell examination, and all types need a 10-year hydrostatic test and thickness gauging. Since 5 Aug 2023 MOM no longer sends owners reminders, so owners have to track due dates themselves, which is a real gap. I found no Singapore product built for this, but the core job is little more than a reminder calendar. AEs already file everything in MOM's WSH eServices and probably remind their own clients. The pain is low: the work comes every 1-2 years and the AE does it. I did not find the penalty or the number of vessels. The idea fits better as a feature inside a broader statutory-equipment tracker.

result.competitor: I found no FEDA-specific compliance or dorm-management SaaS in Singapore. The search turned up MOM's FWMOMCare app (built by NCS, for workers and not operators), the pandemic-era AccessCode on SGWorkPass, and generic overseas products: WelfareAI, Fedena's hostel module and Dormlander (Thailand). Job postings show large operators using unnamed in-house or vendor dormitory management systems, and MOM's NESST Tukang speech mentions an integrated dormitory management system. result.duty: FEDA licence for every foreign-worker dormitory with 7+ beds since 1 Apr 2023, in four classes: 7-99, 100-299, 300-999 and 1000+ beds. It is valid for 3 years, and the renewal goes through GoBusiness at least 3 months before expiry to avoid a late fee. Serious incidents must be emailed to MOM within 3h, with a report within 24h. Changes to licence information must be notified within 14 days, and MOM needs 21 days' notice before an eviction. Changes to directors or structure, and religious, race-related or political events, need MOM's prior approval. The 2022 factsheet adds a resident nominal roll to MOM, plus regular management reports for commercial dorms. I couldn't read the factsheet PDF, so these points come from search snippets. Fees from 1 Apr 2026 are occupancy x $1.50 x years, plus a $100 base fee. Penalty: up to $50,000 and/or 12 months' jail per breach of a licence condition (2019 MOM prosecution release, via search snippet). Set A dorms must meet DTS interim standards by 31 Dec 2030.
result.market: MOM's 2022 estimate was about 1,600 dormitories and 439,000 beds under the expanded FEDA, up from 53. As of June 2024, 78% of foreign-worker dormitories were FEDA-licensed (PQ reply). About 200 construction temporary quarters existed per year (2023 PQ). I found no current breakdown by class. Most of the roughly 1,500 newly licensable dorms are small, employer-run CTQs and factory dorms.
result.reason: The duty is real. FEDA has applied to dormitories with 7 or more beds since 1 Apr 2023. Class 1 covers 7-99 beds, and fees changed again from 1 Apr 2026. Operators must report incidents (3h/24h), changes (14 days) and evictions (21 days), and file renewals 3 months ahead. I found no FEDA-specific SaaS, only generic or overseas dorm software and in-house systems. But most duties are triggered by events, not periodic, and the licence itself recurs only every 3 years. Many licensees are employers (contractors' temporary quarters, factory dorms) handling only a few incidents a year. The market is about 1,500 dorms, and big operators run their own systems. Willingness to pay is likely low. The 2030 DTS interim-standards upgrade deadline is a possible hook.

result.competitor: The MUIS Halal Certification E-Service Portal is free and covers applications, menu and ingredient updates, renewals and status checks. Live QR e-certificates have been issued since 1 Oct 2025. WhatsHalal ATeMS is a Singapore startup platform, live since 2019, that claims to manage the full certificate lifecycle and daily halal assurance bookkeeping. I found no evidence of it after 2020, and it may have refocused on Malaysia and Indonesia, so its current status is unverified. Halal consultancies (HalalHub Consultants, HCS Consultants) prepare documentation and audit readiness. MUIS runs its own HalMQ training and workshops. I found no other Singapore halal records software for eateries.
result.duty: Confirmed in force. Search snippets of the MUIS files HCC EEC1 and EEC2 give Version 4.1, effective 9 Mar 2026. The PDF text could not be extracted, so I did not check clause-level record formats. HalMQ has been compulsory for all MUIS applicants and certificate holders since 1 Jan 2010. You need at least 2 Muslim staff (3 for catering and central kitchens) who pass the Halal Competency Assessment, which has a mandatory refresher. MUIS audits the site, and inspects again after certification. Ingredient documents scale with risk: a questionnaire for low and medium-risk items, a MUIS-recognised certificate for high-risk items. Penalties: rejection or revocation, then a block of at least 90 days before reapplying (v3.0, Dec 2023). Renewals are auto-submitted 120 days before expiry. Digital certificates have been issued since 1 Oct 2025. I did not find how Category 1 differs from Category 2.
result.market: About 4,000+ MUIS halal-certified eating establishments out of about 23,600 retail food establishments, according to Muis as cited by NTU/NIE in May 2026. The count is growing about 10% a year. In 2025, 75% of new and renewal applications were approved. The Category 1 subset is not found, and many outlets belong to chains such as McDonald's, Burger King and Subway that have in-house QA, so there are fewer small independent buyers.
result.reason: The duty is real and in force. MUIS halal conditions for eating establishments, EEC1 and EEC2 v4.1, took effect on 9 Mar 2026. HalMQ has been compulsory since 2010, and a rejection or revocation brings a 90-day blackout before reapplying. But the market is small: about 4,000 certified eateries, many of them chain outlets, and I could not find how many are Category 1. The MUIS portal already handles menu and ingredient updates, applications, auto-renewals and e-certificates. Consultants (HalalHub, HCS) do the documentation work. WhatsHalal's ATeMS (Singapore, live 2019) claims to cover halal record-keeping after certification, but I found no news of it after 2020. Small eateries pay little for this beyond about S$1k per outlet. The opening is narrow and needs a niche: supplier certificate expiry tracking and audit packs.

result.competitor: HACCP/FSMS software listed on Capterra/GetApp Singapore: FoodDocs (builds HACCP plans, daily task checklists), ChefComply (HACCP checklists, temperature logs, audit reports), EazyHaccp (restaurant temperature and cleaning logs), MoreFromFood (digital HACCP, automated temperature monitoring), GoHACCP, HACCP Nexus, Food Guard (IoT temperature alerts). The klikit POS covers SAFE and offers temperature logging. Certification bodies (e.g. TUV SUD for SS 590 / SS 444) and FSC Level 4 (AFHO) training providers (e.g. NYP) serve the certified route. result.duty: The SFA SAFE framework's Phase 1 has been in force since 19 Jan 2026 and grades by track record: A needs more than 3 years with no major lapse. Category 1 establishments (caterers, restaurants with kitchens of 16 m2 or more, in-house kitchens, food processors) can fast-track to A with a 1-year clean record, an Advanced Food Hygiene Officer (AFHO) and a certified FSMS. In Phase 2, an AFHO plus a certified or uncertified FSMS (SS583 counts as uncertified) becomes a requirement for A, with details by 2027 and no start date set. The consequences are grade-related, not fines; a major lapse means an immediate downgrade to C. Separately, caterers must already submit a HACCP-based FSMS referencing SS583:2022, a pre-licensing condition since 1 Jun 2014 that was extended to licences with ancillary catering from 1 Apr 2019. The FSMS is voluntary for restaurants unless they want an A grade.
result.market: About 45,000 SFA-licensed establishments fall under SAFE (SFA). I couldn't find a separate count for Category 1 establishments; it is a subset made up of caterers, larger-kitchen restaurants, in-house kitchens and food processors. The number of licensed caterers was not reached.
result.reason: The SAFE framework is real. Phase 1 has been in force since 19 Jan 2026 for about 45,000 establishments. But for restaurants an FSMS is only a condition for getting or keeping an A grade: it speeds up the route to A in Phase 1 and is needed for A in Phase 2, which can be uncertified. It is not a licence duty, Phase 2 details only come by 2027, and SFA's page names no fines. Caterers already have to submit an SS583-based HACCP FSMS before licensing (since 2014, and since 2019 for ancillary catering), so consultants already serve that need. Generic HACCP apps listed in Singapore (FoodDocs, ChefComply, EazyHaccp, MoreFromFood, GoHACCP) already digitise logs and HACCP plans. I didn't check whether any of them fits SS583 or SAFE.

Duty is real and in force: speed limiters are mandatory on lorries of 3,501-12,000 kg, in phases. The next deadline is 1 Jan 2027 for lorries of 5,001-12,000 kg registered from 2018. Penalty is up to $1,000 or 3 months' jail, and MHA plans to raise the fine to $10,000. Non-compliant lorries cannot be driven or renew road tax, and bizSAFE audits flag them. I found no compliance-tracker product, only hardware and telematics vendors. The weak points are that the duty is a one-off hardware install by one of 61 authorised agents, the PSG grant ends 31 Mar 2027, and the final deadline is mid-2027. About 94% of the earlier cohort (about 2,300 lorries) already complied, so the window is short and the market small. Not recurring, little software value.

The duty is real. NEA requires cooling tower registration (fee $100 per system from 1 Apr 2026) and monthly SAC-lab water testing, with results submitted via ePortal by the 14th of the next month. Duty is real: MOM requires registering air receivers, steam receivers, refrigerating receivers, steam boilers/autoclaves, economisers and superheaters, through an Authorised Examiner. Exams are yearly for boilers and every 2 years for receivers, plus 10-year hydrostatic and thickness tests. Owners must book an examiner before the due date. MOM stopped sending owner reminders from 5 Aug 2023, so a due-date gap exists. Examiners file via the free WSH eServices portal, and owners can only enquire and de-register there. I found no Singapore-specific reminder product, only generic CMMS vendors (Oxmaint, Fabrico). Not checked: fines, and the number of vessels or owners (no count found). The market is small and niche, and the pain is low (a calendar or the examiner's own follow-up covers it). Distribution would need the roughly dozens of examiner firms.
